title: The Ring of Gyges
objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Glaucon asks whether anyone would stay just while wearing a ring of invisibility, and what the challenge asks of ethics.
summary: Glaucon states the view that justice is a compromise kept only for its rewards and challenges Socrates to show it is good in itself, stripped of reputation.

cards.headline: Level 3 gave you the ring. Now meet the challenge it was built for.
cards.body: Glaucon doesn’t actually think injustice is better. His problem is that he has never heard justice defended in a way that satisfies him.

cards.headline: Three kinds of good
cards.body: Glaucon sorts good things into three classes. Some we welcome for their own sake, like harmless pleasures. Some are good in themselves and for their results, like knowledge, sight and health. Some are chores, like exercise, medical treatment and money-making, chosen only for what they bring. Socrates puts justice in the best class, good both ways. Most people, says Glaucon, file it with the chores.

cards.headline: Justice as a deal
cards.body: Then he states the common view. Doing injustice is good for you and suffering it is bad, so people who have tasted both agree to have neither, and make laws. Justice is a compromise between the best, doing wrong unpunished, and the worst, being wronged with no power to hit back. On this view nobody loves justice. They just can’t afford the alternative.

cards.headline: Two lives, polished like statues
cards.body: The ring suggests people are just only when they can’t get away with injustice. Glaucon sharpens it. Picture a perfectly unjust man with the finest reputation for justice, and a perfectly just man thought the worst of men all his life. The just man is stripped of reputation so we can see whether he’s just for justice’s sake or for the rewards. Which one is happier?

cards.headline: What the challenge demands
cards.body: Glaucon asks Socrates to set rewards and results aside and show what justice does, by itself, to the soul of the person who has it. His brother Adeimantus adds: whether seen or unseen by gods and men. Reputation is off the table. That is the challenge for ethics: show that being just is worth it in itself. Plato spends the rest of the Republic answering.

cards.headline: The Ring of Gyges: the big picture
learned: Three classes of good: for itself, for results, or both
The common view: justice is a compromise deal
Two lives: just but scorned, unjust but admired
The challenge: show justice is good in itself

questions.prompt: Match each good with the class Glaucon puts it in.

pairs.right: Good in themselves and for their results

questions.explanation: Harmless pleasures we welcome for their own sake, knowledge is good in itself and for its results, and exercise is one of the chores.

questions.prompt: Why does Glaucon give his perfectly just man a reputation for injustice?

options.label: To show that reputation always lies
So we can tell if he’s just for justice’s sake, not rewards
To prove the just man is secretly unjust and deserves blame
options.rationale: He is perfectly just by design.

options.label: Because the story needs a villain
options.rationale: He is the hero of the comparison.

questions.explanation: Stripping away the rewards of seeming just lets us test whether justice is worth having for its own sake.

questions.prompt: In Level 3, Glaucon argued people are just only when they can’t safely be unjust. Which of his classes of goods does that put justice in?

options.label: Goods chosen only for their results
Goods welcomed only for their own sake
options.rationale: Nobody on this view enjoys justice for itself.

options.label: Goods valued for their own sake and their results
options.rationale: That’s Socrates’ view, not the ring’s lesson.

options.label: A class of goods above all three

questions.explanation: If people are just only from fear of what injustice would cost them, justice is a chore valued only for its results.
